findings.title: Choosing identifier a@acmeshop.dev unlocks internal_tools — this survives turning off client traits.
findings.subject: internal_tools

explanation.title: Anyone can unlock internal tools by picking a staff-style email
explanation.what_happened: The internal_tools flag turns on for any identifier matching the staff rule, such as a@acmeshop.dev. An outsider using the public client key can send that identifier and receive the feature. No account trait is involved.
explanation.why_it_matters: The app trusts a self-declared identifier, which anyone can choose. Turning off trait-based checks does not close this gap.
explanation.business_impact: Unauthorized people could reach internal tooling in Production, risking exposure of internal data and functions.
explanation.fix_summary: Stop matching staff access on a client-supplied identifier. Decide staff status on the server and serve the flag from verified data.

evidence.note: Flagsmith's engine serves on instead of off for flag "internal_tools" to any identity whose identifier matches segment "staff_by_identifier", for example "a@acmeshop.dev". No trait is involved.

findings.title: Secret in a client-visible flag value: payment_config
findings.subject: payment_config

explanation.title: Payment secret exposed in a public feature flag
explanation.what_happened: Using only the public client key, anyone can fetch the payment_config flag in Production. Its value includes a live payment provider API secret (acmepay) and a webhook address.
explanation.why_it_matters: Client keys are meant to be visible in apps and browsers. Secrets stored in flag values are therefore readable by anyone.
explanation.business_impact: Attackers could use the key to act on your payment account, causing fraud, financial loss, and customer data exposure.
explanation.fix_summary: Revoke and replace the exposed secret now, move it to a server-side secrets store, and keep only non-sensitive settings in client-visible flags.

evidence.note: secret detected in value at $.api_secret (acme_live_key)

findings.title: Forging role=admin unlocks admin_panel (segment "admins")
findings.subject: admins

explanation.title: Anyone can switch on the admin panel by claiming to be an admin
explanation.what_happened: The system decides who is an admin based on a "role" value that the caller supplies themselves. A test request using only the public client key and role=admin flipped the admin_panel flag from off to on in Production.
explanation.why_it_matters: The role is self-declared and never verified, so any outsider can claim it. A security control is relying on information the user can fake.
explanation.business_impact: Unauthorized people could be shown admin features, risking exposure of sensitive data or actions, and loss of customer trust.
explanation.fix_summary: Stop deciding admin access from caller-supplied values. Enforce admin rights on the server using verified identity, and treat the flag as display-only.

evidence.note: Flagsmith's engine serves on instead of off for flag "admin_panel" to an identity with trait/identifier role="admin" (segment "admins"; forgeable: yes).

findings.title: Users can pick their own group in experiment "Pricing page price test" (pricing_page)
findings.subject: pricing_page

explanation.title: Visitors can choose their own price in the pricing test
explanation.what_happened: Anyone using the public client key can request the pricing page flag with any identifier they like. By trying different identifiers, they can keep going until they land in the cheaper "price_low" group instead of "price_high". About half of attempts succeed.
explanation.why_it_matters: The experiment assumes users are assigned randomly. Self-selection breaks that, so results become unreliable.
explanation.business_impact: Customers can get lower prices than intended, reducing revenue, and the test may lead to a wrong pricing decision.
explanation.fix_summary: Assign experiment groups on the server using a trusted user ID, not an identifier the visitor supplies, and don't expose assignment control to clients.

evidence.note: Variant spread over 1000 identifiers: map[price_high:489 price_low:511]

explanation.title: Secret payment flag is exposed to apps and browsers
explanation.what_happened: The production flag "payment_config" is classified as secret, but its "Server-side only" setting is off. Because of that, client SDKs receive it, so anyone using the app or SDK key could potentially read it.
explanation.why_it_matters: Secret settings should only reach your servers. Sending this one to client-side code puts it where outsiders can view it.
explanation.business_impact: Payment configuration details could leak, helping attackers target your checkout, enabling fraud, or creating compliance concerns.
explanation.fix_summary: Turn on "Server-side only" for payment_config in the production dashboard. Then review whether its contents were exposed and rotate anything sensitive.

evidence.note: Feature "payment_config" is classified SECRET but the dashboard setting "Server-side only" is off, so client SDKs receive it.

findings.title: Traits of ce***@acmeshop.dev are readable by anyone with the public client key
findings.subject: ce***@acmeshop.dev

explanation.title: Customer traits readable with the public client key
explanation.what_happened: Anyone holding the public client key, which ships inside the app, can request a customer's stored traits by supplying their identifier. In production, one test identity returned 3 traits. Gatecrasher did not read the values.
explanation.why_it_matters: The "Hide sensitive data" setting is off, so the traits are served to anyone who asks. They are classed as personal information, and the client key is not a secret.
explanation.business_impact: Customer personal data could be harvested, creating privacy-law exposure, breach-notification duties, and loss of customer trust.
explanation.fix_summary: Turn on "Hide sensitive data" for the production environment so traits are no longer returned. Remove personal data from traits that don't need to be there.

evidence.note: Identity stores 3 trait(s); "Hide sensitive data" is off, so GET identities/?identifier= returns them. Trait values are not read by Gatecrasher.

findings.title: Traits of qa***@acmeshop.dev are readable by anyone with the public client key
findings.subject: qa***@acmeshop.dev

explanation.title: User profile data readable with a public key
explanation.what_happened: Anyone holding the public client key, which ships inside the app, can request a user's stored profile traits from the production service. The test showed one trait returned for a QA account. Its value was masked in the evidence.
explanation.why_it_matters: The public key is meant to be visible to everyone, so it should not unlock personal data. Anyone could look up users by identifier.
explanation.business_impact: Customer personal data could be exposed, risking privacy complaints, regulatory penalties, and lost customer trust.
explanation.fix_summary: Stop returning identity traits to public client keys, or require a server-side secret key. Then review which traits are stored.

explanation.title: Anyone can self-grant the gold plan and unlock premium export
explanation.what_happened: Using only the public client key, an outsider sent a request claiming their plan was "gold". The system accepted it and switched the premium_export feature on, with no proof of payment or account.
explanation.why_it_matters: The plan level is taken from what the caller says about themselves, so it can't be trusted to gate a paid feature.
explanation.business_impact: Non-paying users can get premium features free, which means lost subscription revenue and weaker incentive to upgrade.
explanation.fix_summary: Decide plan-based access on the server from verified billing data, not client-supplied traits. Don't let client keys set traits used by segments.

evidence.note: Flagsmith's engine serves on instead of off for flag "premium_export" to an identity with trait/identifier plan="gold" (segment "gold_plan"; forgeable: yes).

findings.title: Internal URL leaked to every browser: internal_api_url
findings.subject: internal_api_url

explanation.title: Internal admin address exposed to every browser
explanation.what_happened: Anyone holding the public client key can request the flag list and see a flag named internal_api_url. Its value points to a private network address for an admin interface.
explanation.why_it_matters: The value is meant for internal use only, yet it is sent to every visitor. It reveals how the internal network is laid out and where an admin service lives.
explanation.business_impact: Attackers gain a map for targeting your admin systems, making later attacks easier. It also signals weak separation between public and private configuration, which can worry customers and auditors.
explanation.fix_summary: Remove this flag from the client-facing environment and keep internal addresses in server-side configuration only. Then review other flags for similar internal values.

evidence.note: internal url detected in value at $ (private_ip)

findings.title: Re-rolling the identifier unlocks early_access_ai (≈9% rollout, ~11 tries)
findings.subject: early_access_ai

explanation.title: Anyone can unlock the early AI feature by changing their ID
explanation.what_happened: The early_access_ai flag is meant for a 10% canary group. Because users choose their own identifier, an outsider can try new IDs until one lands in the group. About 9% succeed, so roughly 11 tries are enough, and the flag turns on.
explanation.why_it_matters: The percentage rollout trusts an identifier the caller controls, so it is not a real access control.
explanation.business_impact: Unreleased AI functionality could be seen or used by people who weren't chosen, undermining staged rollouts, risking unfinished features, and skewing canary results.
explanation.fix_summary: Don't rely on client-chosen identifiers to gate unreleased features. Use server-assigned or authenticated IDs, and keep sensitive flags off the client-side key.

evidence.note: Flagsmith's engine serves on instead of off for flag "early_access_ai" to an identity with trait/identifier identifier="gc-probe-map-5" (segment "canary_10"; forgeable: yes).

findings.title: Production: "Allow client SDKs to set user traits" is ON
findings.subject: allow_client_traits

explanation.title: Visitors can fake their own user traits in Production
explanation.what_happened: In Production, the setting that lets client SDKs set user traits is ON. Anyone with the public client key can assign themselves any traits they like.
explanation.why_it_matters: Segments that decide who gets a feature based on a trait can be forged, so access rules can't be trusted.
explanation.business_impact: Outsiders could unlock features, beta access, or paid tiers they shouldn't have. That risks lost revenue and exposure of restricted functionality.
explanation.fix_summary: Turn off "Allow client SDKs to set user traits" in every environment that uses segments for access control. Set traits from your trusted server instead.

evidence.note: Environment "Production": dashboard setting "Allow client SDKs to set user traits" is ON (allow_client_traits). Anyone holding the public client key can set their own traits, so any segment keyed on a trait can be forged. Turn this setting off for every environment that uses segments for access control.

explanation.title: Production feature flag data is not hidden
explanation.what_happened: The 'Hide sensitive data' setting is turned off in the Production environment. This means sensitive values tied to your feature flags are not masked. The evidence shows only the setting state, not whether anyone has actually viewed or taken data.
explanation.why_it_matters: With masking off, anyone who can reach the flag data in Production may see values that should stay private, such as keys or user details. It removes a safety layer.
explanation.business_impact: Sensitive customer or system information could be exposed, risking privacy complaints, loss of customer trust, and possible compliance problems.
explanation.fix_summary: Turn on 'Hide sensitive data' for the Production environment in the dashboard settings, then confirm the setting is saved.

evidence.note: Environment "Production": dashboard setting "Hide sensitive data" is OFF (hide_sensitive_data). Sensitive data is not hidden in this environment. Turn this setting on.

findings.title: Unreleased product leaked through flag: project_nightjar_launch_2026_12_15
findings.subject: project_nightjar_launch_2026_12_15

explanation.title: Secret product launch name visible in public flag list
explanation.what_happened: Anyone holding the client key, which ships inside the app, can request the flag list and see a flag named project_nightjar_launch_2026_12_15. The name reveals a codename and a planned launch date of December 15, 2026. Only the name is exposed; its value was empty.
explanation.why_it_matters: Flag names are readable by outsiders, so internal plans placed in them become public before the announcement.
explanation.business_impact: Competitors, press, or investors could learn about the unreleased product and its timing, weakening launch surprise and giving rivals time to respond.
explanation.fix_summary: Rename the flag to a neutral name with no codename or date, and keep a private mapping internally. Establish a naming rule for future flags.

evidence.note: unreleased product detected in flag name (codename_launch)

explanation.title: Internal API address exposed to client apps
explanation.what_happened: The production flag "internal_api_url" is not marked "Server-side only", so client SDKs receive it. Anyone using the app or SDK can potentially see this internal address.
explanation.why_it_matters: Internal URLs are meant to stay private. Revealing one tells outsiders where internal systems live, which helps them plan attacks. The evidence doesn't show the address itself is reachable from outside.
explanation.business_impact: Low severity, but it leaks infrastructure details and could make targeted probing of internal services easier.
explanation.fix_summary: Turn on "Server-side only" for this flag in the production dashboard so client SDKs stop receiving it. Consider whether the address needs to be changed if it was sensitive.

evidence.note: Feature "internal_api_url" is classified INTERNAL_URL but the dashboard setting "Server-side only" is off, so client SDKs receive it.

explanation.title: Unreleased product flag is visible to client apps
explanation.what_happened: The flag named for an unreleased product launch is not set to "Server-side only" in Production, so client SDKs receive it. Anyone inspecting the app's flag data could see the flag's name.
explanation.why_it_matters: The flag name reveals a project codename and a planned launch date. Sensitive flags should stay on servers, out of public reach.
explanation.business_impact: Competitors or press could learn about the confidential launch plans early, weakening the announcement and the company's competitive timing.
explanation.fix_summary: Turn on "Server-side only" for this flag in Production. Consider renaming it to something neutral that doesn't reveal the project or date.

evidence.note: Feature "project_nightjar_launch_2026_12_15" is classified UNRELEASED_PRODUCT but the dashboard setting "Server-side only" is off, so client SDKs receive it.
